chapter_theme: Back in Vanchi after the northern campaign, the Chera hears through Neelan the Chola's and Pandya's taunts that captives who fled in ascetics' guise are no victory; the brahmin Maadalan calms his anger and preaches that body, wealth and youth pass and the soul goes by its deeds, and urges a Vedic sacrifice in place of the sacrifice of war; the king performs it, frees the prisoners, and installs the Himalayan stone as the pathini's jewelled image with daily worship, while the narrator sums up the three lessons the pathini gave the three kings.

cast.role: the Chera king of Vanchi, returned from the northern campaign with the Himalayan stone (named here குட்டுவன், கோமகன், வேந்தன், வடதிசை வணக்கிய மன்னவர் ஏறு)
the Chera queen's women and attendants
the women of Vanchi who greet the evening and the returned warriors
the Chakkaiyan dancer of Paraiyur who performs Siva's koṭṭicētam
the chief of the chamberlains (கஞ்சுக மாக்கள்) sent to escort the Aryan kings to the Chola and Pandya
the brahmin of Thalaichengaanam, of unfailing learning, who counsels the Chera
the Chola king in his old city, the Chera's cousin (named கிள்ளி in the previous kaathai)
the Pandya now reigning at Madurai after the fire (வெற்றிவேற் செழியன் in the previous kaathai), not the Nedunjeliyan who died
the northern kings beaten by the Chera and paraded before the other two kings
the Chera's officer sent with the revenue accountants
the brahmins of the field of dharma who go with the king to the temple
the skilled artisans who made the image

silappathikaram:28:1-14.reading: At evening in the Chera's old city of Vanchi, women holding white-wicked lamps scatter flower offerings and hail the king of the world, and the warriors with palmyra garlands who finished his war come home with chests pressed by elephant tusks and torn by spear, arrow and sword.
silappathikaram:28:1-14.nuance: The opening sentence does not close in this unit: the list of the warriors' wounds is the object of what the women do with them in the next lines. The wounds are counted by weapon, so the homecoming is told through the body of the fighter, not through the king's victory.
silappathikaram:28:1-14.event: Evening falls on Vanchi; lamp-bearing women hail the king as the wounded warriors return.

silappathikaram:28:15-24.reading: The dark-eyed young women soothe those wounds with the warmth of their breasts, their perfumed hair loosened, their glances shot like Kama's flower arrows, and they praise this evening as both the go-between and the medicine, smiling with fresh smiles.
silappathikaram:28:15-24.nuance: The evening, elsewhere in the tradition the hour when longing hurts, is here called தூதும் மருந்தும் (lines 20-21): it brings the lovers together and heals what war did. The scene sets up, before the brahmin's sermon, the pleasures of a victorious city that the sermon will call passing.
silappathikaram:28:15-24.event: The women of Vanchi tend the returned warriors' wounds with their embrace and praise the evening.

silappathikaram:28:25-38.reading: The mango-leaf-skinned women give their delights to the young men, set mirrors before them to see their hair, garlands and adornment, take up the curved small yaazh and play in the old order of the paalai and kurinji modes like the singing women, and so feast the men as guests, while the narrator begins to liken the coming moon to the face of Kuttuvan.
silappathikaram:28:25-38.nuance: Lines 33-35 use technical terms of tuning (குரல், துத்தம், பாலை, குறிஞ்சி) whose exact sense belongs to the musical lore of the time. The simile at 37-38, the king's face when he protects his people, runs on into the next unit.
silappathikaram:28:25-38.event: The women adorn themselves before mirrors, play the small yaazh and feast the young men.

silappathikaram:28:39-54.reading: The moon rises, worshipped by the world, showing the famed city a face like Kuttuvan's, and takes possession of the moonlit terraces, flower beds, stages, bowers and couches where Kama reigns; and in the jewelled hall of the golden palace that stands in the middle of the walled city like Meru in the middle of the earth, the queen Venmal comes to see the moon's beauty while bangled women carrying lamps spread on one side singing her many years.
silappathikaram:28:39-54.nuance: காட்டி நீங்க (line 40) and வழிமொழி கேட்ப (41) are hard to fix: whether something departs as the moon shows itself, and whose words the men and women hear, is not clear to me. The queen is named only as வதுவை வேண்மாள் மங்கல மடந்தை.
silappathikaram:28:39-54.event: Queen Venmal comes to the jewelled hall of the palace to see the moon, with lamp-bearing women singing blessings.
silappathikaram:28:39-54.unit_note: Boundary moved from 55/56 to 54/55: line 54 closes the first ஒருசார் clause (பரந்தன வொருசார்); line 55's drums and yaazh begin the second, which ends at 56.

silappathikaram:28:55-64.reading: On every side the queen's attendants press round: drums and yaazh and ripe songs on one side, hunchbacks and dwarfs carrying musk and white sandal on another, eunuchs dressed as women carrying colours, powders and garlands on another, flowers, incense and perfume round the couch, and maids carrying mirrors, clothes and jewels.
silappathikaram:28:55-64.nuance: The retinue repeats almost item by item the Pandya queen's train in the twentieth kaathai (mirror, cloth, colours, musk, hunchbacks); here the same splendour surrounds a queen whose city is at peace.
silappathikaram:28:55-64.event: The queen's attendants gather round her with music, scents, garlands, mirrors, clothes and jewels.
silappathikaram:28:55-64.unit_note: Unit cut from the original 56-70: it now starts at 55 (see the previous unit) and ends at 64, the last ஒருசார் clause; line 65 (ஆங்கு) begins the king's ascent with the queen.

silappathikaram:28:65-83.reading: The king who rules the earth ascends the jewelled stage with the queen and watches the koṭṭicētam of the god whose one side is Uma, danced by the Chakkaiyan of Paraiyur of the four-Veda brahmins, with the anklet sounding, the drum beating, the thousand eyes giving their signs and the red matted hair sweeping the quarters on one half while on the other half nothing stirs; pleased, he praises the dancer, goes to the royal hall, and Neelan and the chamberlains come with the brahmin Maadalan, announce themselves through the gatekeepers and bow.
silappathikaram:28:65-83.nuance: The dance shows the god as half woman: the lines on what moves (anklet, drum, matted hair) and what does not (bangle, girdle, breast, earring, hair knot) divide the one body between Siva's fury and Uma's stillness. The Chakkaiyan acts the god's dance; the god himself is not on the stage. A Saiva performance sits in a Chera court that also hears a Vedic sermon and will found a pathini's temple.
silappathikaram:28:65-83.event: The king and queen watch the Chakkaiyan dance Siva's koṭṭicētam; then Neelan and the chamberlains come with Maadalan to the royal hall.
silappathikaram:28:65-83.unit_note: Unit made from 67-70 of the original 56-70 and 71-83 of the original 71-84: it starts at 65 (ஆங்கு, the king ascending) and ends at 83, where the chamberlains bow; line 84 is the vocative that opens Neelan's report.

silappathikaram:28:84-95.reading: Neelan reports that when they reached the Chola's old city and went with the Aryan kings beaten in battle to bow before the Chola, seated in the painted hall gathered from Vajra, Avanti and Magadha, the Chola told his army chief that to take in a winning war those who had flung away sword and umbrella on the field and saved their lives in the guise of men who do not kill is no victory.
silappathikaram:28:84-95.nuance: கொல்லாக் கோலம், the guise of those who do not kill, points back to the end of the Kaal Kol kaathai, where the beaten kings escaped dressed as matted, ash-smeared ascetics, singers and dancers. The Chola's words are a judgment on the Chera's triumph made in the Chera's own envoy's hearing.
silappathikaram:28:84-95.event: Neelan reports that the Chola, shown the captive Aryan kings, said it was no victory to take men who had saved their lives in ascetics' guise.

claims.claim: to take captive in war those who fled the field in the guise of non-killers is no victory

silappathikaram:28:84-95.unit_note: Boundary moved from 84/85 to 83/84 and from 96/97 to 95/96: the unit begins with Neelan's vocative (line 84) and ends at 95, where the Chola's words close with their subject after the verb (உரைத்தனன் ... செம்பியர் பெருந்தகை).

silappathikaram:28:96-109.reading: Neelan goes on: when, after the Chola left, they showed the Aryan kings on elephants under the umbrellas taken from them to the Madurai king, the Pandya Cheliyan said that the conquest of a man who turned his burning anger on those who, having bowed to the god whose half is Uma on the Himalaya's peak, gave up the field to the king and took the great guise of penance, was a new kind of victory; and Neelan tells all these long words of the two kings.
silappathikaram:28:96-109.nuance: புதுவது, 'new', is ironic: a victory over men who had already renounced is no victory. The Pandya calls the Chera கொதியழற் சீற்றம் கொண்டோன் (106), the burning-fire anger the patikam and this kaathai's line 219 give to Kannaki's breast. The Pandya here is the new king at Madurai after the fire, not the Nedunjeliyan who died.
silappathikaram:28:96-109.event: Neelan reports the Pandya's taunt that defeating kings who had put on ascetics' guise was a strange victory.

claims.claim: burning anger turned on those who have taken the guise of penance wins no honour

silappathikaram:28:96-109.unit_note: Boundaries moved from 96/97 to 95/96 and from 112/113 to 109/110: the unit runs from the turn to the Pandya (ஆங்குநின் றகன்றபின், 96) to the close of Neelan's report at 109 (நீலன் கூற).

silappathikaram:28:110-122.reading: Hearing it, the king's lotus eyes turn the colour of fire and he laughs; Maadalan of unfailing learning rises, hails him as king of kings, and recounts his victories: Viyalur of the small-stemmed neythal destroyed, nine kings beaten in the standing battle at the Neri gate, the camp outside Idumbil, the sea driven back, and the Aryan kings who came against him beaten at the Ganges.
silappathikaram:28:110-122.nuance: The laugh is anger, not amusement, as the next unit's 'let your anger subside' shows. Maadalan begins with praise before he counsels; the list of victories is close in wording to the preface of the fifth decad of the Patitruppattu.
silappathikaram:28:110-122.event: The king's eyes redden and he laughs in anger; Maadalan rises and recounts his victories.
silappathikaram:28:110-122.unit_note: Boundary moved from 112/113 to 109/110: the unit now opens with the king's anger and laugh (110-111) and Maadalan's rising (112), which lead into his speech; it ends at 122 as before.

silappathikaram:28:123-138.reading: Maadalan asks the king, a bull among kings who understands with the wise, to let his anger rest, wishes him days more than the sands of the Porunai, and asks him to hear without scorn: after fifty years of guarding the world he has nowhere performed the sacrifice of the field of dharma, only the sacrifice of the field of war; and he begins to list the king's ancestors, the one who cut the kadamba in the sea, the one who carved the bow on the mountain, the one who took a four-Veda brahmin's poem and sent him to the upper world.
silappathikaram:28:123-138.nuance: அறக்கள வேள்வி against மறக்கள வேள்வி (131-132) turns the bards' old figure of battle as a sacrifice against the king: his wars were a sacrifice of the wrong kind. The fifty years, ஐயைந்து இரட்டி, use the same count as the gold Maadalan received in the last kaathai. The blessing by the sands of a river is an old formula (Purananuru 9 ends with the sands of the Pahruli).
silappathikaram:28:123-138.event: Maadalan bids the king calm his anger and tells him he has performed only the sacrifice of war, never the sacrifice of dharma.

claims.claim: a king who has made only the sacrifice of the battlefield, never the sacrifice of dharma, has left his duty undone

silappathikaram:28:139-154.reading: Maadalan finishes the list, the one who held back Death bidding it take lives only in order, the one who ruled the land of the harsh-tongued Yavanas and entered the golden mountain, the one who destroyed Agappa, the one who bathed in Ayirai and the two seas, the one who brought the crossroads spirits into Vanchi and offered the honey sacrifice, and says that since none of these exalted ones remains the king knows the body does not last, and that he has seen from the Aryan kings who scorned Tamil that wealth does not last.
silappathikaram:28:139-154.nuance: The ancestors are named by feats, not names; several of the feats (Agappa, Ayirai, the two seas, the bow on the Himalaya, the kadamba) are those of the Patitruppattu's prefaces. The proof that wealth passes is the king's own victory over the Aryans: his triumph is turned into a lesson against triumph.

claims.claim: the body does not last, as no great king of the past remains
wealth does not last, as the fall of the conquered kings shows

silappathikaram:28:155-170.reading: Maadalan adds that the wise need not tell the king youth does not last, since he sees his own greying body, and that, as those of unfailing sight teach, a good soul that came in a god's form may turn into a human one, a soul wearing a human body may enter a beast's, and a soul in a beast's body may come among the hell-dwellers, for like dancers the soul does not stay in one costume but goes by the way of the deeds it did; and he blesses the king's wheel of rule.
silappathikaram:28:155-170.nuance: The four states, gods, humans, beasts and hell-beings, are the scheme of the Jain gatis, but the text names no school: a brahmin cites them as the word of பொய்யில் காட்சியோர். The introducing phrase பொய்யில் ... பொருளுரை is the formula the brief cites from Manimekalai 22 for a Kural quotation, but what follows here is not a Kural couplet. கோலம், costume, is the word the kaathai used of the Aryan kings' disguise (92, 105).

claims.claim: the soul passes between the bodies of gods, humans, beasts and hell-beings, going by the deeds it did, as a dancer changes costume

silappathikaram:28:171-180.reading: Maadalan says he is not one who seeks rich gifts, but cannot bear that the king, beyond the poets' measure, should go the common way by which lives leave this world; the brahmin of sacrifice learned in the four Vedas will open to him the way the gods praise, and he must perform the great sacrifice that the Veda sets for kings, for if he says he will do dharma tomorrow, a life rich in learning may leave today.
silappathikaram:28:171-180.nuance: Maadalan disclaims the gift-seeker's motive just after (in the last kaathai) the king gave him gold by weight. The 'dharma' that must not be deferred is here a Vedic royal sacrifice performed by priests, not the giving or conduct the ethical books usually mean.
silappathikaram:28:171-180.event: Maadalan urges the king to perform the great Vedic sacrifice without delay.

claims.claim: a king should perform the great Vedic sacrifice, which opens the way the gods praise
dharma must not be put off to tomorrow, for life may leave today

silappathikaram:28:181-186.reading: Maadalan ends: no one in the old world has known the fixed span of his days, so may the king, with this lady of the sacrifice, guard the world aeon upon aeon while crowned kings praise his feet, and live long.
silappathikaram:28:181-186.nuance: The sermon on impermanence closes, as court speech must, with a wish for a reign of aeons; the queen is called வேள்விக் கிழத்தி because a king performs the sacrifice with his wife.
silappathikaram:28:181-186.event: Maadalan closes his counsel with a blessing on the king and queen.

claims.claim: no one knows the fixed span of his life

silappathikaram:28:181-186.unit_note: Unit cut from the original 181-201: it ends at 186, where Maadalan's speech closes (நெடுந்தகை யென்று).

silappathikaram:28:187-206.reading: The brahmin having ploughed with his Veda tongue and sown its meaning in the field of the king's ear, the harvest ripens: the king, wishing to enjoy it, orders the Veda-learned priests to hold the sacrifice and its festival as Maadalan prescribed, frees the Aryan kings from prison, lodges them in the Velavikko mansion in the park outside Vanchi, and tells Villavan Kothai to send them home after the sacrifice and do for them what befits kings, orders the prisons opened everywhere and the towns' taxes remitted, and sends Azhumbil Vel with the revenue accountants through the city.
silappathikaram:28:187-206.nuance: The narrator's ploughing figure (187-189) endorses the sermon: it bears fruit at once in acts of clemency. The release of prisoners and remission of dues are the usual festival acts of a king, here prompted by a lesson on impermanence.
silappathikaram:28:187-206.event: The king orders the sacrifice, frees the Aryan kings and all prisoners, and remits the towns' taxes.
silappathikaram:28:187-206.unit_note: Unit made from 187-201 of the original 181-201 and 202-206 of the original 202-214: no sentence ends between 187 and 234, so it closes at 206 (ஏவி), the last of the orders of release, before the pathini clause begins at 207.

silappathikaram:28:207-221.reading: The narrator recalls the pathini whom the world worships: she gave the garlanded Chola the proof of the ancients' Tamil saying that unless kings rule justly the chastity of famous women does not shine, gave the southern king the lesson that a king does not live once his sceptre bends, gave the western king the lesson, made known to the northern kings, that kings' fierce anger does not cool until their vow is fulfilled, and, having ruined old Madurai with the burning anger she brought forth from her breast, came to the good land and stood in the shade of the flowering vengai.
silappathikaram:28:207-221.nuance: The three lessons go one to each crowned king and do not match the patikam's three morals: karma is absent, and the third is about the Chera's own vow. What 'gave to the Chola' means (that her chastity's glory waited on the Pandya's justice being tested, or that the Chola learned it from her story) is not plain to me, and I mark the reading uncertain. The phrase கொதியழற் சீற்றம் கொங்கையின் விளைத்து repeats the patikam (line 44).

claims.claim: unless kings do justice, the chastity of renowned women does not shine
a king does not live on once his sceptre bends
kings' fierce anger does not cool until their vow is fulfilled

silappathikaram:28:207-221.unit_note: Unit made from 207-214 of the original 202-214 and 215-221 of the original 215-234: it holds the whole relative clause on the pathini, closing at 221 on its object நங்கையை; line 222 turns to the king's going to her temple.

silappathikaram:28:222-234.reading: The king who bent the north goes with the brahmins of the field of dharma, the teacher, the great astrologer and the skilled artisans, worships the god of the Himalaya's peak, and in the pathini's temple laid out by men of the texts has the divine image carved by masters adorned with every jewel, offers flowers, sets guards at the door, ordains sacrifice and festival every day, and commands that the goddess's auspicious rite be done.
silappathikaram:28:222-234.nuance: The kaathai is named நடுகல், the hero-stone; the stone fetched from the Himalaya becomes a jewelled image in a temple with Brahmin priests and daily sacrifice, so the old warrior's stone is turned into a goddess's shrine. This fulfils the patikam's உரைசால் பத்தினிக்கு உயர்ந்தோர் ஏத்தல்.
silappathikaram:28:222-234.event: The king installs the jewelled image of the pathini in her temple and ordains daily sacrifice, festival and worship.
silappathikaram:28:222-234.unit_note: Unit cut from the original 215-234: it starts at 222, where the king's own acts begin, and ends at the kaathai's close.

links.note: The beaten Aryan kings fled the field disguised as matted, ash-smeared ascetics, singers and dancers; here the Chola names that disguise கொல்லாக் கோலம் and denies the Chera any glory for taking them.
links.teaches: The ruse that saved the northern kings' lives in battle becomes, in the rival Tamil kings' mouths, the reason the Chera's triumph counts for nothing, so the escape and the taunt together show a victory spoiled by the vanquished's change of dress.

links.note: Puram 9 praises a Pandya who before battle bids cows, brahmin-natured men, women, the sick and the sonless take shelter; the Chola's dictum spares, after battle, men who have made themselves look like non-killers.
links.teaches: The old dharma of war spares people by what they are, but the epic shows warriors claiming that shelter by what they wear, and a king using the rule not to restrain himself but to belittle another king's captives.

gains.a: the Chola's taunt gains its ground: an old Tamil rule that war is not waged on those who do not fight
gains.b: the poem's list gains a hard case it does not foresee, defeated fighters who step into the spared class by disguise

links.note: Maadalan's list of the king's victories runs close to the wording of the fifth decad's preface on Senguttuvan: சிறுகுரல் நெய்தல் வியலூர், இடும்பின் புறத்து இறுத்து, the nine kings beaten at the gate in standing battle, the sea driven back, the Aryan beaten at the Ganges.
links.teaches: The preface's bare record of conquests, which names the pathini's stone only as its occasion, becomes in the epic the praise a brahmin recites to cool the king's anger just before telling him that such conquests pass, so the same list serves first as glory and then as the premise of a sermon on impermanence.

gains.a: the epic's list gains an independent Sangam witness for the same campaigns in nearly the same words
gains.b: the preface's terse கடவுள் பத்தினிக் கற்கோள் gains the story of who the pathini was and what the stone became

links.note: After the northern battle the Chera is hailed as one who made a field of dharma (அறக்களஞ் செய்தோன்) having finished the field of war; Maadalan tells him he has made only the war-field sacrifice and never the dharma-field one.
links.teaches: The epic sets the battlefield hailed as a field of dharma against a brahmin's verdict that the same wars were sacrifice of the wrong field, so the king's highest praise and his counsellor's rebuke use the same two words to opposite ends.

links.note: Among the ancestors Maadalan cites are the king who took a four-Veda man's poem and sent him to the upper world, and (lines 144-146) the one who struck Agappa and bathed in Ayirai and the two seas; the third decad's preface and colophon give Palyanai Selkezhu Kuttuvan these feats and the brahmin poet's reward of heaven through sacrifices.
links.teaches: The Sangam tradition's sacrifice that sent a brahmin poet to heaven becomes Maadalan's precedent for the sacrifice he urges on the king, yet the same preface says that king went away to the forest, and the epic's counsellor leaves out the renunciation and keeps only the rite.

gains.a: Maadalan's allusions gain the stories behind them: the poet Gautamanar, his reward and the king who gave it
gains.b: the preface gains a later reading in which its king's sacrifice is remembered and his going to the forest is not

links.note: The couplet ranks not killing one creature to eat above a thousand oblations; Maadalan ranks the sacrifice of dharma above the war-sacrifice in which the king has killed for fifty years.
links.teaches: Read together they make a three-step ranking that neither states: the Kural puts abstaining from killing above the Vedic rite, while the epic's brahmin puts the Vedic rite above the killing of war and offers it as the remedy for that killing.

gains.a: Maadalan's remedy is shown to rest on a ranking the Kural itself would not grant
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where the oblation is urged as the cure for killing, not as its rival

links.note: Both tell a king that the rulers before him, many and mighty, are all gone; Puram 363 concludes that he must renounce the whole sea-bounded world before death, Maadalan that he must perform a great sacrifice and rule for aeons.
links.teaches: The same proof from dead kings yields opposite counsel: the Sangam poet's impermanence ends in giving up the kingdom, the epic's brahmin's in a rite that keeps the king on the throne, so the argument alone does not decide between renunciation and ritual.

gains.a: Maadalan's sermon is seen to stop short of the conclusion the older poem draws from the same premise
gains.b: the poem's call to renounce is set against a counsellor who uses its argument for a royal sacrifice

links.note: The patikam opens with the Chera prince Ilango, who gave up kingship and lives at the eastern gate; here a Chera king is told that body and wealth do not last and is led to a sacrifice, not to the forest.
links.teaches: Within one royal house the epic shows the two answers to impermanence, the prince who left the throne and the king who is counselled to stay on it and sacrifice, without saying which is right.

links.note: The Naladiyar quatrain calls the life a dancer (கூத்தன்) who leaves the skin bag, after which the body's fate does not matter; Maadalan's soul is like dancers who do not stay in one costume but go by their deeds into the bodies of gods, men, beasts or hell-beings.
links.teaches: The quatrain uses the dancer to make the abandoned body worthless, while the epic follows the dancer to its next costume, which its deeds choose, so the same figure moves from indifference to the corpse to anxiety about the next birth.

gains.a: Maadalan's simile gains a known ethical use of the dancer image to test against
gains.b: the quatrain's dancer gains a destination: the epic says where the performer goes after leaving the costume

links.note: The beaten Aryan kings escaped as ascetics and as dancers (ஆடு கூத்தர்) in a changed guise (விச்சைக் கோலம்); Maadalan tells their conqueror that the soul too is like dancers who change their கோலம்.
links.teaches: The kings' change of costume to save their lives, mocked by the king's rivals, returns in the sermon as the image of every soul's passage from body to body, so the mockery of the disguised kings recoils on the mocker.

links.note: In the previous kaathai the king gave Maadalan gold to his own weight, counted as ஐயைந்து இரட்டி; here Maadalan says he is not one who seeks rich gifts.
links.teaches: The counsellor's disclaimer comes after the largest gift in the story, so the epic leaves the reader to weigh whether the sermon is disinterested, without itself saying so.

links.note: The couplet says do aram without saying 'later'; Maadalan says if the king says 'we will do aram tomorrow', life may leave today, and the aram he means is the Vedic royal sacrifice.
links.teaches: The epic keeps the couplet's urgency but narrows aram from the whole of virtue to one rite performed by priests for a king, showing how the ethical maxim could be recruited for a particular religious practice.

gains.a: Maadalan's urgency gains the authority of a general rule about not deferring virtue
gains.b: the couplet's unspecified aram is shown filled with one school's content in a court setting

links.note: The patikam's three morals are that dharma becomes death to kings who err, that the great praise a pathini, and that former deeds come to fruit; here the pathini gives three lessons, one to each crowned king.
links.teaches: The epic's late summary turns the patikam's morals into lessons addressed to the three kings and drops karma for the Chera's fulfilled vow, so the story's close weighs kingship more than the former deed the patikam put among its causes.

links.note: The couplet gives the wife who worships her husband power over the rain on her own; the ancients' saying quoted here makes the glory of famous women's chastity depend on kings doing justice.
links.teaches: The couplet's chastity commands nature unaided, but the epic's closing saying makes its public glory wait on the king's justice being tested, so the pathini's power is tied to a failure of the sceptre.

gains.a: the saying is set against the best-known claim for a chaste wife's unaided power
gains.b: the couplet gains a condition the Kural does not state: chastity's power shows itself through the state's justice or injustice

links.note: The Chera vowed that unless he took a stone for the goddess on the heads of the northern kings his sword should be counted shameful; here the narrator says the pathini taught the western king that kings' anger does not cool until their vow is fulfilled.
links.teaches: The Chera's vow, made in anger at reported scorn, is in the end credited to the pathini as one of her lessons, so the king's campaign is retold as her teaching rather than his own design.

links.note: Puram 264 tells of a hero-stone set up on gravelly ground, crowned with a red flower garland and peacock feathers, with the fallen man's name carved; the epic's kaathai named நடுகல் installs a stone from the Himalaya as a jewelled image with priests and daily rites.
links.teaches: The epic takes the hero-stone rite, raised by herdsmen for a fallen fighter, and gives it to a woman whose power is chastity, enlarging it with Brahmin sacrifice and a temple, so the old rite of the warrior becomes the founding of a goddess's cult.

gains.a: the kaathai's title gains its source in the rite it adapts: stone, garland, offering
gains.b: the poem's simple rite is shown transformed into temple worship of a pathini

new_concepts.gloss: the sacrifice: the Vedic rite performed by priests for a patron, and by extension a deed spoken of as a sacrifice (the battle as மறக்கள வேள்வி)
the chaste wife whose steadfastness gives her word power over kings, cities and nature

source_issues: The kaathai has 234 lines in the core file but the edition's printed last line number is 230; the four-line difference is in the edition's numbering, and this file uses the core file's line numbers.
Line 115 reads வியுலூ ரெறிந்தபின்; the place is வியலூர் in the Patitruppattu's fifth preface, so வியுலூர் is probably a misprint.
Line 40 (காட்டி நீங்க) and line 41 (வழிமொழி கேட்ப) are hard to construe; unit 39-54 is marked uncertain.
